description: Hi everyone! I’m Aaron Delgado, an Electromechanical Engineer passionate about astronomy, space exploration, and data-driven systems. Why join my team? We will merge physical systems, smart analytics, and creative execution into a solid, functional prototype. If you want to work on a high-impact space concept with a structured, collaborative, and results-oriented approach, this is the place.
summary:
PlanetX Atlas is a free, public web tool that lets anyone type a star name or sky coordinates and instantly see real SPHEREx images of that region, played as a video across observation dates, to spot objects that move or change brightness. Users can blink, slide, subtract and stack epochs, overlay Gaia DR3, WISE, SIMBAD, any VizieR catalog or their own CSV, follow a source through every frame and extract a 102-channel SPHEREx spectrum in seconds. Each candidate is checked against known stars and JPL’s list of known asteroids, so users see whether it is already catalogued before treating it as new.

We tested it on the challenge targets. The tool recovered the measured proper motions of Barnard’s Star and Epsilon Indi B, detected brightness changes in RW Aurigae and R Draconis, and tracked asteroid 16 Psyche within 2″ of JPL’s predictions. WISE 0855 is too faint for a single SPHEREx exposure, and the tool reports that result as inconclusive.

When a moving dot turns out to be an asteroid, users can follow it into a 3D Solar System of 1.58 million real orbits. There they can see what is known about its composition, with evidence levels, and how hard it is to reach.

This turns SPHEREx’s enormous dataset into something volunteers can explore, helping more people contribute to discovering new worlds.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

PlanetX Atlas is a free public web tool that turns NASA SPHEREx images into a "time machine" for the sky. Anyone can type a star name or coordinates (decimal or sexagesimal) and instantly see real SPHEREx exposures of that region from different dates, played as a video on a common north-up grid. Real dates and gaps between observing seasons are shown honestly, and frames are never interpolated.

Users can blink two epochs, compare them with a slider, subtract them to reveal what moved, or stack them to improve signal-to-noise. Quality flags, wavelength and provenance (link to the original FITS file) are shown for every frame. Overlays from Gaia DR3, CatWISE, SIMBAD, any VizieR catalog, or the user's own CSV are propagated by proper motion to each frame's date. Known asteroids are predicted with JPL's Small-Body Identification service. In "Planet X mode" the user clicks a source, the tool follows it through all dates, fits its motion, and classifies it with explicit criteria: known asteroid, known high proper-motion star, possible variable, probable artifact, or unidentified candidate that needs review. A 102-channel SPHEREx spectrum is extracted in about 3 seconds by reading only the needed bytes of the SPHEREx HiPS cube with HTTP range requests.

FROM A MOVING DOT TO A MISSION DESTINATION

When the moving dot is an asteroid, the user can follow it into a live 3D Solar System of 1,582,561 real asteroid and comet orbits, propagated on the GPU. A prospecting module ranks 7,212 NASA NHATS-accessible near-Earth asteroids with a transparent, adjustable-weight index. Each object gets a composition card that labels every fact as observed, calculated, inferred, illustrative or unknown, including ground truth from OSIRIS-REx, Hayabusa2 and DART. Our own Lambert solver computes launch-window "porkchop" plots, and a 3D/WebXR explorer lets users visit the asteroid at real scale. A planetary-defense tab adds CNEOS close approaches, Sentry and fireballs.

SCIENTIFIC VALIDATION

We validated the tool on the challenge targets using real SPHEREx data:

- Barnard's Star and Epsilon Indi B: proper motion measured with 2D-Gaussian centroids registered against Gaia stars, consistent with the catalog values.

- RW Aurigae and R Draconis: brightness changes detected.

- Asteroid 16 Psyche: tracked within 2 arcseconds of JPL's predictions in 12 of 12 frames.

- WISE 0855: honestly reported as inconclusive, because it is too faint for single SPHEREx exposures.

We also noticed that the challenge's WISE 0855 coordinates correspond to the WISE epoch, so the tool propagates every target's proper motion to the observation date. Ten more objects are preloaded, and users can save their own cases.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

It lowers the barrier for volunteers, students and researchers to explore SPHEREx data, in the spirit of Backyard Worlds. It connects discovery with real mission planning, and it never presents a visual difference as a confirmed discovery or a taxonomy as a resource estimate.

TOOLS

Python (FastAPI, Astropy, astroquery, astropy-healpix, NumPy, SciPy), TypeScript (React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Three.js, React Three Fiber, WebXR, Aladin Lite), a GPU shader that solves Kepler's equation for 1.58 million bodies, pytest (13 tests, including a Lambert check against a textbook example), Playwright and FFmpeg for the demo video. It runs locally on Windows and as a static online showcase on GitHub Pages.

CREATIVITY AND FACTORS CONSIDERED

Every number carries its evidence level and source, cached snapshots show their date, and the app keeps working when archives are down. It is accessible without registration, works without a VR headset, and is open source.
